teaser: “I could have done that.” Maybe. But there are two hidden paintings under this square.
review_notes:
Malevich's phrase 'zero of form' (from his 1915 manifesto): quoted as two words only.
First shown at the 0,10 exhibition in Petrograd, December 1915, hung across the upper corner like an icon.
2015 Tretyakov Gallery study: two earlier compositions under the black, and a handwritten inscription in the white margin read as a reference to Alphonse Allais's all-black joke picture of the 1890s (a battle in a cave at night). The reading and its authorship are debated.
Cause of the cracks (black applied over layers not fully dry): the usual explanation, check wording.
The 'ghost shapes' spot interprets the smooth and crackled zones visible in the image as traces of the underlying compositions: plausible, but a conservator's confirmation would be welcome.
At least four versions exist (1915, about 1923, 1929, early 1930s); the lesson says 'at least three more'.
Funeral in 1935: black square on the front of the truck carrying the coffin in Leningrad.
Soviet period: kept in storage and rarely exhibited until the 1980s.
Size about 79.5 x 79.5 cm. Malevich's age in 1915: 36.

lesson.text: A black square on a white ground. No subject, no depth, nothing a ruler and a pot of paint could not supply. People have been saying “I could have done that” in front of this painting for more than a century. Fair enough. So try a better question: why had nobody done it before 1915?

Kazimir Malevich was 36, living in Russia in the middle of the First World War, and he had already worked his way through every modern style: Impressionism, Cubism, Futurism. Each still showed things, however broken up: a guitar, a face, a man sharpening knives. He wanted to know what would be left if the things were taken out completely.

He named the answer Suprematism: painting in which pure feeling is “supreme”, more important than any object shown. The Black Square was its starting point. Malevich called it the “zero of form”, the spot where the old art of imitating the world stops and something else can begin.

At its first showing, in Petrograd in December 1915, Malevich hung the square high up across a corner of the room, tilted toward the visitors. Every Russian understood the gesture: that corner is where an Orthodox home keeps its holy icon.

So it was never meant as a prank or as decoration. It was closer to a new kind of icon, an object to stand in front of. And the real object, about 80 centimeters (31 inches) on each side, holds a surprise for anyone who knows it from books: it is not the flat, perfect, printed square you carry in your head.

lesson.title: What a logo leaves out
lesson.text: Three places where the idea turns back into paint.

spots.title: The cracks
spots.text: The black has split into a web of cracks, like dried mud, and paler colors glint through the gaps. Malevich painted over layers that were not fully dry, so the surface pulled apart as it aged.

spots.title: Ghost shapes
spots.text: Some zones are smooth, others crackled, with straight borders between them: a slanting band, an upright strip. They look like the outlines of shapes lying underneath the black.

spots.title: The edge
spots.text: No ruler here. The border between black and white wavers slightly, drawn by hand, and the white is brushed on in visible strokes. Even the square is not perfectly square.

lesson.text: Those ghosts are real. In 2015 researchers at the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow X-rayed the picture and found not one but two earlier compositions under the square, both full of colored shapes. Malevich did not start from nothing. He buried his own previous work, literally, under the black.

The same study found a handwritten note in the white margin. Researchers read it as a nod to a French prank of the 1890s: an all-black picture by the humorist Alphonse Allais, captioned as a battle in a cave at night. Who wrote the note, and why, is still argued over.

After 1915 the square followed him everywhere. He painted at least three more versions and signed some late works with a tiny black square instead of his name. When he died in 1935, a black square was fixed to the front of the truck that carried his coffin through Leningrad.

By then Stalin's government had declared abstract art useless to the people, and the Black Square spent decades in storage, rarely shown in the Soviet Union until the 1980s. Abroad, its descendants multiplied: the single-color canvases of the 1950s, Minimalism in the 1960s, and a good share of modern graphic design.
The Black Square matters less for how it looks than for what it allowed: after it, a painting no longer had to be a picture of anything.

So, is it art? You could not have painted it in 1915, because the idea was the hard part, and the idea was his. But Malevich wanted more than your agreement. He wanted you to stand in front of a black surface and feel something without being shown anything. Does that happen to you? Only the real, cracked object can settle it.

quiz.question: What did Malevich call the style that began with the Black Square?
quiz.explanation: Suprematism puts pure feeling above any depicted object.

quiz.question: Where did he hang the painting at its first exhibition in 1915?
options: High across a corner, like an icon
quiz.explanation: The upper corner is where Orthodox homes keep their icon.

quiz.question: What did X-rays reveal in 2015?
options: Two earlier compositions under the black
quiz.explanation: The square covers two older paintings full of colored shapes.

quiz.question: Why is the black surface covered with cracks?
options: It was damaged in a fire
The black was painted over layers that were not fully dry
quiz.explanation: The layers dried at different speeds and the surface pulled apart with age.

facts.text: The Black Square is a perfectly flat, perfectly geometric square.
facts.explanation: Its edges waver, it is not exactly square, and the surface is cracked.

facts.text: A black square was displayed on the truck at Malevich's funeral.
facts.explanation: It was fixed to the front of the truck that carried his coffin in 1935.

facts.text: Malevich painted only one Black Square.
facts.explanation: He painted at least three more versions after 1915.
